standard.title: First Nations artists celebrate and challenge Australian identity
standard.description: investigate the ways that First Nations Australian artists celebrate and challenge multiple perspectives of Australian identity through their artworks and visual arts practice
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have explored how First Nations Australian arts continue and revitalise cultures, and engaged with site-specific and community-based works (AC9AVA8E02, implied from progression). They understand arts as ongoing cultural practice. They have not yet engaged with First Nations Australian visual arts as explicitly political, activist or identity-challenging, or investigated 'first contacts' and colonisation from multiple perspectives within this frame.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate ways that First Nations Australian artists celebrate and challenge multiple perspectives of Australian identity through their artworks and visual arts practice.

nodes.label: Visual arts as activism
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate how First Nations Australian artists use visual communication as a tool for activism — expressing calls for change through artworks, protest posters and street art.
nodes.minimum_width: Examine one example of First Nations Australian visual art as activism (protest poster, street art, campaign); explain what change is being called for and how visual choices communicate the message.
nodes.typical_width: Research artworks, protest posters and street art by First Nations Australian artists used as activism; analyse how visual communication tools express calls for change; investigate the relationship between visual choices and activist purpose.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian artists are caring for Country/Place through visual arts campaigns — explore how environmental activism is visualised and who the intended audience is
Compare protest posters by First Nations Australian artists from different historical periods — analyse how visual communication strategies have evolved and what stays constant
nodes.hinge_reason: The activist dimension is the key new conceptual territory at Y9-10 compared to earlier bands. Students who only understand First Nations Australian arts as cultural continuation and celebration cannot engage with the challenging and political dimensions the descriptor requires.

response_modes.reason: Students may not have encountered First Nations Australian visual arts as explicitly political. Structured investigation (what change is being called for? who is the intended audience? how do visual choices serve the activist purpose?) builds the analytical framework needed.

success_criteria: Examines at least one example of First Nations Australian visual art as activism
Explains what change is being called for and how at least one visual choice communicates the message

nodes.label: Multiple perspectives on Australian identity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate how First Nations Australian artists present multiple perspectives of Australian identity — including perspectives that challenge dominant narratives about 'first contacts' and colonisation.
nodes.minimum_width: Investigate one First Nations Australian artwork that presents an alternative perspective on Australian identity or history; explain how it challenges a dominant narrative.
nodes.typical_width: Compare and analyse artworks by diverse First Nations Australian artists that celebrate and challenge concepts and histories of Australian identity; investigate 'first contacts' from multiple perspectives; examine how artists present multiple ways of understanding shared histories.
wider: Analyse how First Nations Australian artists use their practices to challenge and inform community debate about 'first contacts' between First Nations Peoples and British or European colonisers — compare with other cultural perspectives
Investigate contemporary First Nations Australian designers who are challenging concepts and histories of Australian identity in commercial and applied design contexts

response_modes.reason: Students who examine only one perspective on Australian identity cannot understand how First Nations Australian artists challenge narratives. Engaging with both the dominant narrative and the challenge — and with multiple First Nations perspectives — is essential.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The intersection of First Nations Australian perspectives on 'first contacts', colonisation and contemporary identity is one of the most complex and significant areas of Australian social history — students who engage deeply with this develop sophisticated historical and cultural understanding.
success_criteria: Investigates at least one First Nations Australian artwork that presents a perspective on Australian identity
Explains how it celebrates or challenges a specific aspect of how Australian identity has been understood

nodes.label: Cultural continuation, development and community voice
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate how First Nations Australian visual arts provide opportunities to continue and develop culture, communicate lived experiences, and care for Country/Place and people.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two distinct ways First Nations Australian visual arts serve community or cultural purposes (continuation, challenge, caring for Country, communicating lived experience).
nodes.typical_width: Explore the full range of ways First Nations Australian visual arts function — cultural continuation, community development, lived experience communication, Country/Place care, identity declaration and political challenge; synthesise understanding across multiple artists and forms.
wider: Work with representatives of the First Nations Australian community to explore how local groups are caring for Country/Place — investigate how visual arts campaigns highlight environmental issues for local and broader audiences

Investigate how the digital age has expanded opportunities for First Nations Australian artists and designers to continue and develop culture — explore specific examples of online, social media or digital art contexts

response_modes.reason: Activism, identity challenge and cultural continuation come together in a complete understanding of First Nations Australian visual arts as simultaneously political, cultural and community-directed — serving multiple purposes at once.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two distinct purposes served by First Nations Australian visual arts (from continuation, challenge, Country care, lived experience communication)
Demonstrates understanding that these purposes are not separate but often simultaneous in a single artwork or practice
